scope: Twenty-one practice questions corrected during local author review: ten introductory items, one reaction-time item, and ten items identified during a browser course challenge. Existing IDs, answer indices, and aggregate progress are preserved. Other bank items remain draft material. Independent subject review remains pending.

previousItems.q: A friend asks what researchers actually mean by 'cognition.' Which answer gets the definition right?
options: The brain's regulation of automatic bodily functions such as breathing, heartbeat, and digestion
Taking in sensory information about the world and processing it in order to decide how to act
The storage of past experiences so they can be consciously relived later in vivid detail
The generation of emotional reactions that color how events are experienced
previousItems.explain: Cognition names the intelligent work of gathering sensory input, interpreting it, and using it to choose actions. Automatic bodily regulation falls below the intelligence threshold, while emotion generation and memory replay alone are each far too narrow to serve as the definition.
previousItems.hint: Think input-to-action: what comes in through the senses, and what does the organism do with it?

previousItems.q: Which of these everyday processes falls outside what researchers count as cognition?
options: Recalling exactly where you parked the car this morning
Following a friend's story at a loud party
Planning the fastest route to work
Your stomach adjusting acid levels after a meal
previousItems.explain: Cognition refers to intelligent mental activity — remembering, attending, planning, understanding. Automatic physiological housekeeping like digestion runs without any of that intelligence, so it sits outside the category alongside functions like breathing.
previousItems.hint: Ask which process would carry on identically even if the person were not thinking at all.

previousItems.q: One researcher studies how healthy adults effortlessly recognize hundreds of faces; a colleague studies face blindness after brain injury. What marks the first project as characteristic cognition research?
options: It targets the machinery that normally runs smoothly and unnoticed, rather than what happens when the system breaks
It avoids the brain entirely, restricting itself to observable social behavior in natural settings
It concerns perception, and disorders can never inform theories of perception
It recruits far larger participant samples, which has always been the defining methodological signature of cognitive research
previousItems.explain: The study of cognition centers on processes that go right — the smooth, largely invisible operations behind ordinary competence. Work on breakdowns is valuable and can inform theory, but the field's core question is how typical minds succeed at what they do every day.
previousItems.hint: The contrast is not about method or sample size — it is about studying success versus studying breakdown.

previousItems.q: Richard Feynman kept the motto 'What I cannot create, I do not understand' on his blackboard. Applied to the mind, what does this motto license researchers to conclude?
options: Because working models of the mind remain out of reach in key areas, our understanding of cognition is still incomplete
Because computers exist, human thought has effectively been explained
Understanding must always come before building, so AI engineering ought to pause until the psychology of thought is finished
Creation and understanding are unrelated, so machine progress says nothing about the mind
previousItems.explain: If genuine understanding implies the ability to build a working model, then our inability to construct machines with humanlike flexibility is diagnostic: it exposes how much about cognition remains unexplained. AI progress thus doubles as a measuring stick for the science.
previousItems.hint: Run the motto in reverse: what does failing to build something imply about understanding it?

previousItems.q: In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, and many predicted machines would soon master everyday human abilities. Why did that leap never happen?
options: Chess turned out to be far harder than ordinary abilities like conversation, so the prediction had the difficulty ordering backwards
Deep Blue won through rapid brute-force evaluation of possible moves — the style of computation machines already excelled at — not through flexible intelligence
IBM classified the underlying method, preventing other engineers from extending it to new domains
Kasparov's defeat was later shown to be a statistical fluke across the full match
previousItems.explain: Deep Blue's victory came from checking the outcomes of possible moves at enormous speed, much like the fast simple operations behind arithmetic. That approach thrives in a fixed, rule-bound domain such as chess but does not transfer to the open-ended situations of everyday life.
previousItems.hint: Ask how the machine won, not whether it won — the method sets the limits on generalization.

previousItems.q: An early chatbot answers 'How are you today?' flawlessly but collapses when asked 'So, how's life been treating you?' What does this failure reveal about its design?
options: It was trained on too small a body of text to develop genuine comprehension of conversational questions
Its sound-processing front end failed, although its understanding of meaning remained fully intact underneath
It understood the question but had no sufficiently polite response stored for that phrasing
It matches anticipated input strings to pre-written replies, so unanticipated phrasing finds no match — no understanding is involved
previousItems.explain: Classic chatbots run on if-this-then-that programming: a recognized string of characters triggers a canned reply. Nothing in such a system grasps meaning, so a paraphrase the programmer never anticipated simply fails to trigger anything, however similar its intent.
previousItems.hint: The two questions mean the same thing but share few words — why would that matter to this machine?

previousItems.q: A robotics firm builds arms that assemble engines with superhuman precision, then fails for years to build a robot that tidies ordinary kitchens. Which principle best predicts this pattern?
options: Pre-programmed machines thrive in fixed, constrained environments but fail where novel situations cannot be specified in advance
Precision manufacturing demands more intelligence than housework, so the firm's talent was aimed at the harder problem first and exhausted there
Kitchens are physically larger than assembly stations, and robot sensors cannot cover spaces of that size reliably
Household tasks require emotional bonds with owners that industrial machines are unable to form
previousItems.explain: An assembly line barely changes from one case to the next, so every contingency can be written down beforehand. A home serves up endlessly novel arrangements — objects moved, lighting shifted, clutter everywhere — and no programmer can enumerate them all, which demands a flexibility machines have historically lacked.
previousItems.hint: Compare how predictable each environment is from one moment to the next.

previousItems.q: You recognize your own phone instantly whether it is face-down in shadow, half-covered by a napkin, or viewed from an odd angle. Why do vision researchers call this feat computationally profound?
options: Phones are deliberately designed to be maximally recognizable from every possible viewpoint and lighting condition
The image the object casts on the retina differs virtually every time, so recognition cannot work by matching exact stored patterns
Recognition of personal possessions is driven by emotional attachment rather than by visual processing
The eye transmits a perfect three-dimensional replica of the whole scene, and the hard work lies in compressing that replica for storage
previousItems.explain: Angle, distance, lighting, and occlusion change the retinal image constantly — the odds of receiving the same image twice are essentially zero. The brain solves this effortlessly, while machine vision struggled with it for half a century, revealing how deep 'simple' seeing really is.
previousItems.hint: Think about what actually lands on the retina across those three situations — is it ever the same twice?

previousItems.q: Recent leaps in AI — vision systems, speech interfaces, large language models like ChatGPT — share a common break with older software. What is it?
options: They run on quantum processors rather than conventional silicon chips
They were each hand-written by enormous teams of expert programmers who anticipated and explicitly coded every conceivable case in advance
They learn from data and feedback, adjusting their own behavior, instead of following rules a human wrote for every condition
They restrict themselves to narrow domains where every situation can be listed beforehand
previousItems.explain: The machine-learning revolution replaced hand-authored if-this-then-that rules with systems trained to improve at a task — many of them neural networks inspired by the brain. Large language models, for instance, are trained on vast text collections plus feedback from their users.
previousItems.hint: The shift concerns where the program's behavior comes from: a human's rules or the system's own training.

previousItems.q: For decades computer models of the mind drew limited attention from researchers of biological intelligence, yet lately that attention has surged. What changed?
options: Computers finally became fast enough to simulate every neuron in a human brain exactly
Brain-inspired models began achieving humanlike performance on tasks once seen as a bare minimum for real intelligence
Modeling stopped borrowing from neuroscience entirely, which made the resulting models far simpler for psychologists to interpret
New regulations required every psychology study to include a simulation component
previousItems.explain: Earlier models could not handle tasks most would call minimally intelligent, so they stayed a niche interest. Modern neural-network systems — built on principles borrowed from the brain — now succeed across many domains, making them newly serious tools for understanding biological minds.
previousItems.hint: The models earned credibility by finally doing something — ask what that something was.

previousItems.q: A researcher pilots a reaction-time study with a single trial per condition. A colleague warns that one sneeze could wreck the results. What is the standard fix, and why does it work?
options: Screen out distraction-prone participants with an attention questionnaire administered before the experimental session
Instruct participants to respond more carefully so no aberrant trials occur
Switch from reaction time to accuracy, which is immune to momentary lapses
Run many trials per condition and average them, so rare aberrant trials contribute negligibly
previousItems.explain: Behavioral data are noisy: lapses, slips, and distractions add variability unrelated to the manipulation. Averaging over many trials exploits the statistical fact that larger samples better estimate true means, letting the occasional bad trial wash out instead of driving the result.
previousItems.hint: The remedy is statistical, not a matter of participant discipline.

previousItems.q: In people who lose their sight — even in adulthood — the occipital cortex starts responding to touch and sound. What does this reorganization demonstrate?
options: A region's function is shaped by the input it receives, a property called neuroplasticity
The occipital lobe was always primarily an auditory area in every person
Without visual input, occipital tissue simply falls dormant and plays no further role in cognition
Vision is not localized anywhere in particular in the cortex
previousItems.explain: Cortical tissue is built from similar circuitry everywhere, so what a region does depends heavily on what arrives there. Deprived of visual signals, occipital cortex gets recruited by hearing and touch — often sharpening those senses. The region does vision because it receives visual input, not the reverse.
previousItems.hint: Flip the causality: does the region choose its input, or does the input define the region?

previousItems.q: Listeners shadowed the sentence 'The boys threw rocks at the bank' while the word 'money' repeated in the ignored ear (Mackay, 1973). Later they interpreted the sentence as being about a financial bank — yet denied ever hearing 'money.' What does this pattern show?
options: Ignored input is stored in conscious memory at first but is completely forgotten within about a minute of presentation
Ignored input can be processed for meaning and bias interpretation without ever reaching awareness
Ambiguous words are always resolved toward their most frequent everyday sense
Shadowing is too demanding for listeners to comprehend the attended sentence
previousItems.explain: The ignored word steered which sense of 'bank' listeners settled on even though it never became conscious, so semantic processing occurred outside awareness. A filter that discarded unattended input before meaning could not produce this bias, showing that filtering is far more flexible than strict early models claim.
previousItems.hint: Separate two questions — was the word consciously heard, and did its meaning nonetheless have an effect?

previousItems.q: A colleague insists that constant juggling of chat, email, and spreadsheets has made him an expert multitasker. Based on task-switching research, what is the most likely reality?
options: Frequent multitaskers tend to show the largest switching costs, so his habit may have made him worse
He is probably right, since research shows switching efficiency improves steadily the more often people juggle tasks in daily life
Switching costs vanish for anyone once the individual tasks become familiar
His overall speed is unchanged, but his accuracy has probably improved
previousItems.explain: Multitasking usually amounts to rapid task switching, and each switch carries a time cost while the mind reconfigures. Strikingly, the heaviest habitual multitaskers show the biggest switching deficits, so confidence in one's own multitasking is a poor guide to actual performance.
previousItems.hint: The relationship between how often people juggle tasks and how well they switch is not the intuitive one.

previousItems.q: What pattern do 'use it or lose it' literacy and numeracy graphs illustrate?
options: High and low use produced identical age-skill curves
Low use preserved skills better than frequent use did
All skills increased equally regardless of engagement
High use preserved skills; low use declined more
previousItems.explain: The displayed profiles associated high reading or math use with stronger maintenance across age, while low-use profiles peaked and then declined more.
previousItems.hint: Compare the red high-use curves with the dashed blue low-use curves.

previousItems.q: Which evidence types support the conclusion that multiple memory systems have different properties?
options: Brain scans, genetics, and clinical drug trials
Experiments, behavior records, and observations
Philosophy, introspection, and computer benchmarks
Surveys, interviews, and intelligence rankings alone
previousItems.explain: Conclusions about different kinds of memory come from experiments, behavioral recordings, and observational reports.
previousItems.hint: Choose the three empirical sources listed before capacity and duration were introduced.

previousItems.q: Reed (1974) had people memorize a Star-of-David-like figure, then asked from memory whether a parallelogram had been part of it. Accuracy on that probe was poor, though probes like the component triangles were easy. What did Reed conclude?
options: Images decay too quickly during the retention interval to support part-verification from memory at all
The figure was too visually complex to encode in a single viewing
Participants had mentally rotated the figure, distorting the embedded shapes
People had stored a structural description like two overlapping triangles, not a depictive image
previousItems.explain: If the memory were truly picture-like, any embedded shape should be recoverable from it, the way it is from a drawing on paper. Success only for parts named in a plausible verbal description — triangles yes, parallelogram no — points to a labeled, descriptive code.
previousItems.hint: Ask which parts a short verbal label of the figure would mention.

previousItems.q: Given a mixed set of items to remember, people typically recall those presented as pictures better than those presented as words. What is this phenomenon called?
options: The concreteness effect
The generation effect
The depictive encoding advantage
The picture superiority effect
previousItems.explain: Memory reliably favors pictures over words — the picture superiority effect. Paivio's dual coding account says a picture is stored twice, as an image and as a verbal label, doubling the retrieval routes, while a word usually receives only the verbal code.
previousItems.hint: The name states exactly which format wins in memory.

previousItems.q: A veteran engineer and a first-year hire both face a design problem whose best solution violates standard practice in their field. Who is more likely to find it, and why?
options: The veteran, because deeper expertise reliably improves solution quality across all problem types
The veteran, because automatic processing conserves capacity that can be redirected toward generating novel ideas
The first-year hire, because novices have superior working memory capacity
The first-year hire, because no entrenched mental set steers them toward conventional approaches
previousItems.explain: Deep experience builds strong mental sets and automatic responses; those usually help, but when a problem demands abandoning standard practice they steer experts down familiar roads. Lacking those ruts, a newcomer can be freer to consider unconventional options — the situation where expertise becomes a liability.
previousItems.hint: This particular problem punishes exactly what years of expertise build up.

previousItems.q: A computer beats any human at the Tower of Hanoi, yet the information-processing approach still treats human and machine solvers as usefully comparable. What is the key processing difference behind the performance gap?
options: Computers use heuristics while humans rely on exhaustive algorithms
Humans cannot represent the problem's changing states at all
Computers can evaluate all possible moves at once, while limited working memory lets humans hold only a few candidate steps
Machines lack executive control processes, so nothing slows down their search
previousItems.explain: Both humans and machines combine incoming information with stored memory under a limited-capacity central processor, which is why the comparison is fruitful. The gap is capacity: a computer can churn through every legal move, while human working memory holds only a handful of possibilities at a time — forcing people onto heuristics where machines run exhaustive algorithms.
previousItems.hint: Both are processors of information — compare how many possibilities each can juggle at once.

previousItems.q: After bilateral vmPFC damage, patients in Bechara et al.'s (2000) card-gambling study kept choosing decks with big immediate payoffs and larger long-run losses — while stating they knew the strategy was bad. How does the somatic marker hypothesis explain this?
options: vmPFC damage erases explicit memories of the previous losing hands
vmPFC damage abolishes the capacity to reason about long-term outcomes, so patients can no longer understand which strategy is optimal
Without the vmPFC, the gut emotional signals that normally tag risky options never arise, so knowledge fails to steer choice
vmPFC damage heightens anxiety so much that patients become too fearful to abandon familiar decks
previousItems.explain: Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis holds that the vmPFC attaches bodily emotional signals — a flutter of anxiety, a warning gut feeling — to options under consideration. Lesions sever that channel, so intact abstract knowledge never receives the visceral tag needed to guide the actual choice.
previousItems.hint: The patients' knowledge was intact; ask what signal failed to accompany it.

previousItems.q: In the modal-model diagram, which set of transitions is correctly matched with its process?
options: Sensory input to sensory memory by retrieval; STM to LTM by attention
Sensory memory to STM by encoding; LTM to STM by rehearsal
Attention to STM; encoding to LTM; retrieval back to STM
Sensory memory to LTM by attention; LTM to STM by maintenance
previousItems.explain: The diagram shows attention moving selected sensory information into STM, encoding moving STM information into LTM, and retrieval bringing LTM information back into STM.
previousItems.hint: Trace the arrows in both directions around short-term memory.

previousItems.q: The resource-pool figure showed capacity falling from simple colored squares to Chinese characters, random polygons, and shaded cubes. What principle does this pattern illustrate?
options: Visual STM always holds exactly seven items
Complex items use more of a limited STM resource
Only familiar stimuli can ever enter visual STM
Stimulus complexity affects duration but never capacity
previousItems.explain: The figure treats capacity as a limited pool: simple colored squares permit more items, whereas structurally complex objects consume more resources per item.
previousItems.hint: Compare how much processing each object demands, not just how many objects appear.

previousItems.q: Which age-related pattern was shown in the cognitive-performance graph?
options: World knowledge declines fastest, while processing speed rises
All cognitive measures remain flat from the twenties to eighties
Working memory rises sharply while long-term memory disappears
Speed, WM, and LTM decline; world knowledge is more preserved
previousItems.explain: The graph showed declining speed of processing, working memory, and long-term-memory performance with age, alongside comparatively preserved vocabulary-based world knowledge.
previousItems.hint: The orange/red vocabulary lines followed a different trajectory from the speed and memory lines.

previousItems.q: Which pattern of information loss matches the modal-model diagram?
options: Only sensory memory loses information over time
Rehearsal removes STM information, while long-term memory is always permanent
Unattended sensory input, unrehearsed STM, and some LTM can be lost
Attention erases sensory input while retrieval erases LTM
previousItems.explain: The diagram shows unattended information dropping from sensory memory, unrehearsed information dropping from STM, and some information being lost from LTM over time.
previousItems.hint: Each storage stage has a different route by which information can fail to persist.

previousItems.q: In the place-cell figure, an ordered firing sequence unfolds across about six seconds while a rat is active and reappears across about two-tenths of a second while it sleeps. What is the best interpretation?
options: Sleep erased the active sequence and replaced it with unrelated cell firing.
The active sequence was replayed during sleep in a temporally compressed form.
The sleeping sequence proves that temporal order is irrelevant to consolidation.
The rat converted spatial procedural memory into a consciously declared fact.
previousItems.explain: The same ordered place-cell pattern appears during sleep on a much shorter timescale. This is the figure's example of faster hippocampal replay that preserves sequence order after the original experience.
previousItems.hint: Compare both the order of colored cells and the time axes.

previousItems.q: In the bird-picture naming graph, experts favored specific labels such as 'sparrow' or 'robin,' whereas nonexperts favored the basic label 'bird.' What does this show?
options: The basic level is preferred equally by experts and nonexperts in every categorization task
Experts lose access to basic categories
Expertise can shift naming from the basic level toward subordinate labels
Nonexperts rely mainly on superordinate labels
previousItems.explain: The visual figure shows that the basic level is the common default for nonexperts, but specialized knowledge makes more specific subordinate labels useful and accessible to experts.
previousItems.hint: Compare which naming level each knowledge group used most often.

previousItems.q: What is the role of the Innocence Project?
options: Training witnesses to increase confidence before trial
Using DNA evidence to exonerate people wrongly convicted after eyewitness testimony
Replacing all lineups with autobiographical interviews
Preventing investigators from collecting physical evidence
previousItems.explain: The Innocence Project is described as lawyers using DNA evidence to overturn wrongful convictions based on eyewitness testimony. Since 1982, 350 cases have been overturned, and an estimated 100,000–200,000 people have been wrongly convicted because of eyewitness testimony.
previousItems.hint: The organization checks remembered identification against biological evidence.

previousItems.q: Which experience has been associated with working-memory improvements in young children?
options: Repeated articulatory-suppression sessions
Computerized tone-cue practice
Musical training
Memorizing randomly arranged chess pieces
previousItems.explain: In work by Gui et al. (2018), musical training was associated with improved working memory in young children.
previousItems.hint: The example involved structured artistic practice.

previousItems.q: Action potentials are all-or-none — there are no big or small spikes. How, then, does a neuron convey that one stimulus is stronger than another?
options: By firing action potentials at a higher rate
By generating taller electrical spikes
By switching to a different type of neurotransmitter
By sending its signal down extra axons
previousItems.explain: Since every spike is identical in size, intensity lives in timing: stronger drive produces more frequent firing, and this rate of action potentials is the vocabulary neurons use with one another. A given neuron also releases only one neurotransmitter, so it cannot switch chemicals to signal strength.
previousItems.hint: If every spike is the same size, what else about spiking can vary?

previousItems.q: Which example most directly describes physiological regulation rather than the cognitive processes emphasized in this lesson?
options: Recalling exactly where you parked the car this morning
Following a friend's story at a loud party
Planning the fastest route to work
Your stomach adjusting acid levels after a meal
previousItems.explain: Stomach acid regulation is the physiological example. Remembering a location, attending to speech, and planning a route directly illustrate cognitive processes. Automaticity alone is not the distinction: cognition can also operate with little conscious effort.
previousItems.hint: Focus on the kind of process described, not whether it feels effortful.

previousItems.q: How did Miller assess auditory STM capacity in the study described?
options: Participants matched two pictures after a delay
Participants repeated ordered verbal lists in sequence
Participants recalled a cued row from a letter grid
Participants counted backward while retaining a trigram
previousItems.explain: Miller presented ordered lists of verbal items and asked participants to repeat them in order, revealing a stable individual span.
previousItems.hint: This was a span task using ordered verbal material.
